title: A case report of pulmonary paragonimiasis diagnosed via the deterioration of pulmonary cavities during high-dose corticosteroid therapy for chronic eosinophilic pneumonia
case_text: A 32-year-old Chinese woman presented to our hospital with a cough and bloody sputum. Twelve months before presentation, the patient developed a dry cough. Eight months before presentation, she visited another hospital with a cough and bloody sputum and underwent chest radiography, which revealed a bilateral infiltrative shadow [Figure 1a]. She was diagnosed with CEP due to >80% eosinophilia in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid. The patient was treated with corticosteroids. Methylprednisolone was administered intravenously at 125 mg/day for 3 days, followed by oral prednisolone at 25 mg/day; prednisolone was reduced by 5 mg/day every 2 weeks. Her symptoms improved. Seven months before presentation, chest radiography, and chest CT showed improvement in the bilateral infiltrative shadows [Figures 1b and 2a]. However, 5 months before presentation, the bilateral infiltrative shadow worsened and pulmonary cavities appeared at 10 mg/day of oral prednisolone therapy [Figures 1c and 2b], which was increased to 20 mg/day. One month before presentation, the left lung cavities worsened at 20 mg/day of oral prednisolone therapy [Figure 1d]; thus, transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) and BAL were repeated. Although TBLB showed nonspecific findings, Paragonimus ova was found in the BAL fluid [Figure 3]. Laboratory tests revealed normal eosinophil count (222/muL). The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary paragonimiasis. Prednisolone therapy was tapered. When she was referred to our hospital, she experienced a relapse of dry cough without bloody sputum at 5 mg/day of oral prednisolone. The patient came to Japan 9 years ago and had a custom of eating freshwater crabs in China. Her vital sign was stable. Physical examinations revealed no remarkable findings. Laboratory tests revealed normal white blood cell count (7270/muL), eosinophil count (370/muL), and C-reactive protein level (0.13 mg/dL). Chest radiography showed deterioration of the bilateral infiltrative shadows [Figure 1e]. The patient showed no abnormal findings on brain magnetic resonance imaging. One week after the initial visit, oral prednisolone therapy was discontinued. Two weeks after the initial visit, her symptoms, such as cough and bloody sputum, worsened, and chest radiography revealed deterioration of the bilateral infiltrative shadow [Figure 1f]. Laboratory tests revealed elevated eosinophil counts (1290/muL). Treatment with praziquantel (75 mg/kg/day) for 3 days was initiated. Three weeks after the initial visit, although her symptoms improved, a transient skin rash was observed in the lower abdominal region. Five weeks after the initial visit, follow-up chest radiography showed improvement in the bilateral infiltrative shadow [Figure 1g]. Blood eosinophil counts gradually decreased (860/muL). Moreover, follow-up chest radiography 3 months after treatment showed further improvement in the bilateral infiltrative shadows [Figure 1h]. Laboratory tests revealed normal eosinophil counts (200/muL). The patient's condition remained stable without recurrence of pulmonary paragonimiasis.

   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.

   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:

   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Foodborne Trematodes
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: pulmonary paragonimiasis
